parsed_answer.content:
In Core Java and fundamental object-oriented design, a class cannot extend more than one class. Java strictly prohibits multiple inheritance for classes to avoid the catastrophic architectural issues famously known as the Diamond Problem. If class D extends both class B and class C, and both B and C override a method from a shared parent class A, the JVM and compiler would face an ambiguous resolution path regarding which implementation of the method, state, or constructor chaining sequence to inherit. By enforcing a single-inheritance model at the class level, Java maintains a clean, hierarchical type tree where every class has exactly one direct superclass, defaulting implicitly to java.lang.Object if no explicit 'extends' clause is declared.

However, Java provides a sophisticated escape hatch for design patterns requiring multiple behavioral facets through the implementation of interfaces. Unlike classes, a Java class can implement multiple interfaces, thereby acquiring behavior contracts without inheriting state or ambiguous constructor overhead. Furthermore, since Java 8, interfaces can contain default methods, which reintroduces the potential for method collision if a class implements two interfaces defining the exact same default method signature. In such scenarios, the Java compiler enforces explicit resolution by forcing the developer to override the conflicting method in the implementing subclass and explicitly invoke the target interface's implementation using the 'SuperInterface.super.methodName()' syntax.

items: Class Single Inheritance: The 'extends' keyword accepts only a single target class, guaranteeing a linear, predictable inheritance hierarchy rooted at java.lang.Object.
Constructor Chaining: Single class inheritance guarantees that 'super()' calls follow an unambiguous path up the call stack to initialize state sequentially.

Interface Multiple Inheritance: A class can implement an arbitrary number of interfaces, and interfaces themselves can extend multiple other interfaces simultaneously without ambiguity because they lack instance state.
Default Method Collision Rules: If a class implements two interfaces with identical default methods, the compiler forces an override to resolve the Diamond Problem explicitly.

parsed_answer.content: A common interview pitfall is confusing class inheritance with interface implementation. While Java developers often state 'Java does not support multiple inheritance,' it is more precise to say 'Java does not support multiple class inheritance.' Through interfaces and default methods, Java actually embraces a controlled form of multiple inheritance of behavior, requiring explicit conflict resolution to keep the type system sound.
